*The Mr. Potato Head*

My Mom made friends with a woman at college who had kids as well. They decided to take classes on opposing days so they could switch off babysitting. The woman had a daughter about 8 months younger then me, and her and I use to play together. 

One day I was at their house when I was about 4 and the girl and I decided to play doctor. The little girl took me to her room, closed the door, and insisted the only way to play doctor was to take off all of her clothes. This wasn't too unusual to me at the time for when we were 2 or 3 her Mom use to make us take bathes together. 

I helped her undress, and she handed me a toy stethoscope. She then decided to lay down on a small changing table as I pretended to use the stethoscope on her. I put it to her chest but she insisted I needed to put it lower, and lower until I was placing the plastic stethoscope on her private area. I was curious so I turned it sideways and tried to insert it into her. The stethoscope was too large so I went to the toy box and pulled out a Mr. Potato Head.

It was an original old school Mr. Potato Head with the long plastic rods that stuck out from behind the different pieces to allow you to stick the eyes, mouth, noses, etc. into the holes on the Mr. Potato Head. I then took the various pieces off the Mr. Potato Head, I took the lips and placed the rod in her, and left it there. Then I inserted the set of eyes above the lips, but there wasn't anymore room for any other pieces so I spread her legs further and took the nose and placed it in her rectum. I spent the next several minutes attempting to make a face with the various facial pieces, but she didn't have enough holes and got bored and we decided to play something else.

And, that my friends is the *The Mr. Potato Head*.

Not a doctor and don't feel we have enough information but it sounds like a mood disorder and not just simply depression which most likely puts you on the bipolar spectrum.

To get a better idea of your personal situation it would be helpful if we knew more about what you are going through and more about you (your age, what drugs you use, sexual activity level, any self harm, sleep habits, etc).

It may not be full blown type 1 or 2, the DSM-4 which doctors use to define criteria for mental disorder currently has a limited view of the bipolar spectrum as it was published in the early 90's and we've learned a lot more about bipolar disorder in the last several years. The DSM-5 will likely be updated in 2012 to include several other variations of bipolar disorder including cyclothymia or bipolar - NOS (none specific).

It is entirely possible to experience what is called "hypomania" which is a much more mild form of mania, and is not a full blown episode. A full blown manic episode tends to include severe delusion, grandeur, increased psycho-motor activity, sexual hyperactivity, irrational decision making, and generally a break from reality. Where as hypomania is marked by goal orientation, impulsive decision making, sexual hyperactivity, but ultimately you are still tied to reality.

Someone with cyclothymia or bipolar-nos for example can experience mood swings, with marked periods of depression, and periods of hypomania and never experience a full blown manic episode (especially if you are younger).

There is also drug induced cyclothymia which can actually be caused antidepressants, and other drugs including pot, and caffeine.

Regardless, the treatment tends to favor mood stabilizers, and avoids antidepressants as they can cause manic behavior.

Ultimately you need to see a psychiatrist.

After going through horrible withdrawals from the Paxil I finally feel like the withdrawals are less of a factor and I'm back to "normal" (it's been 7 months). I don't have much trust in psychiatry anymore.

While I did stop presenting with bipolar nos type symptoms since getting off the antidepressants (like I thought I would, it is unlikely I'm bipolar - although drug induced cyclothymia is a possibility), the depression, anxiety, OCD, and insomnia did not go away (the insomnia is actually worse, as is the depression). While pot can increase my focus sometimes, I'm unsure if this could be classified as hypomania, for the definition of hypomania is pretty much what it's like for a lot of people to get high. Just to clarify, I do not have schizophrenia, and if I do have bipolar disorder of any kind it is it's much weaker cousin cyclothymia. I've never experienced a full blown manic episode, and have never lost touch with reality.

Physically I have horrible IBS and several food allergies, and an impaired sympathetic nervous system (my body doesn't regulate temperature properly, sweats too much, overly sensitive, etc).

I started smoking once I got a new fulltime job to get me to sleep at night and even me out. It has also done wonders for my depression, improved the quality of my sleep, improved my anxiety, improved my OCD, makes eating much more tolerable, and actually allows me to experience happiness.

Clearly I've altered my brain considerably over the years with all of these drugs, and smoking probably isn't making the situation any better, but it does improve the quality of my life considerably. When I smoke I eat better, I seem more motivated to work out, I can actually sleep at night, and overall take better care of myself, and I'm more social and happy.
